# Oil Leaking from Radiator: Diagnosing the Head Gasket and Coolant System

Oil flooding out of a radiator in a 1998 Chrysler Concorde is not merely a leak; it indicates a catastrophic breach between the lubrication system and the cooling circuit. While you have already identified and replaced a cracked oil cooler hose, the fact that the engine still cannot hold oil suggests the failure has migrated upstream to the internal seals or downstream components within the cylinder head assembly.

In this specific vehicle generation, the architecture relies on an integrated oil cooler housed directly within the radiator core. When high-pressure oil escapes this unit, it enters the coolant passages. Because oil is hydrophobic and significantly less dense than water-based coolant, it does not simply mix homogeneously. Instead, it pools at low points in the system or rises to the surface, creating a visible film of oily sludge on top of the coolant reservoir or a thick, dark emulsion resembling chocolate milk in the radiator itself.

The most probable culprit remaining is the head gasket failure. In the 1998 Concorde, as with many engines of that era utilizing pushrod V6 or V8 architectures, thermal cycling causes the aluminum cylinder head to warp over time. As the engine heats up and expands unevenly, microscopic gaps open between the combustion chamber and the coolant/oil galleries. Under pressure from combustion strokes, oil is forced through these gaps into the water jacket.

### Internal Oil Cooler Failure

Even after replacing the external hose, the internal component of the oil cooler remains a prime suspect. The oil cooler consists of a heat exchanger matrix sandwiched between the engine block and the radiator tank. Over 25 years of operation, the internal seals that separate the oil channels from the coolant channels can degrade due to thermal fatigue or chemical attack from old coolant additives.

Diagnosing this requires isolating the source. If you have drained the cooling system and found no oil residue outside of the hose connection point, yet oil continues to appear in the radiator, the breach is internal. You must check for pressure buildup in the oil cooler itself. A common diagnostic step involves checking the coolant temperature sensor reading against actual water temperature; an oil leak into the coolant often alters the thermal mass and specific heat capacity of the fluid mixture, causing the engine to run slightly hotter than expected.

### Blockage and Circulation Issues

A secondary failure mode associated with this symptom is the clogging of the radiator's internal passages. Oil mixed with coolant creates a viscous sludge that traps debris like rust flakes or scale. This sludge restricts flow through the narrow tubes of the oil cooler and the radiator core. When flow is restricted, pressure differentials increase, forcing oil out through any available weak point, such as a compromised gasket seal or a micro-fracture in the aluminum casting.

To address this, simply flushing the system may not be sufficient if the sludge has hardened into a cast within the oil cooler matrix. The technical decision here is whether to attempt a chemical flush or replace the entire oil cooler assembly. Given the age of the vehicle and the cost of labor to remove the radiator for internal inspection, replacing the coolant-to-oil heat exchanger unit is often the more reliable engineering solution.

### Final System Integrity Check

Before committing to a full head gasket replacement, which involves removing the cylinder heads on a 1998 Concordeâa labor-intensive process requiring precise torque sequencing and surface preparationâyou must rule out external coolant-to-oil cross-contamination. Verify that the oil filter is not also saturated with coolant, as this can mask the true source of the leak. If the oil appears milky throughout the pan and the dipstick shows consistent emulsification even after a drained-and-refilled cycle, the internal integrity of the cylinder head is compromised beyond simple hose replacement.

Understanding the fluid dynamics between these two systems helps prevent recurring failures. Oil in the radiator reduces cooling efficiency, leading to overheating, which further warps the head and exacerbates the leak. Addressing the root cause requires replacing the oil cooler assembly if the internal seals are worn, or repairing the head gasket if combustion gases or oil are crossing into the coolant passages from the cylinder block itself.
